name: Maxillary distraction osteogenesis
lead: Maxillary distraction osteogenesis (MDO) is a surgical technique for advancing the upper jaw gradually. The bone is cut, a distraction device is attached, and the segments are slowly separated so new bone forms in the gap, rather than moving the jaw in one step as in conventional orthognathic surgery.[11][12] For appearance, the goal is a more forward upper jaw and midface: more cheek and upper-lip support, a fuller facial profile and a bite that fits, in people whose maxilla sits well behind the lower jaw.

Its main published use is severe maxillary hypoplasia, especially in cleft lip and palate. Early reports from the late 1990s described rigid external devices used in children and adolescents with severe deficiency, with the authors citing both aesthetic and functional benefits.[1][2][3][4] It has also been used in combination with mandibular distraction in hemifacial microsomia.[5] The slow, staged advance lets soft tissue stretch with the bone, which is why surgeons use it for large advancements that are hard to achieve in a single step.

Studies have compared it with orthognathic surgery in cleft patients for morbidity, relapse and five-year stability.[6][7] A 2018 Cochrane review, as summarized by Wikipedia, found only one small study (47 participants) on maxillary distraction in cleft lip and palate, insufficient for general conclusions, although distraction gave greater forward advancement and less horizontal relapse at five years.[11] In looksmaxxing contexts it is mentioned as a more extensive alternative to Le Fort I advancement.

paras: Wikipedia traces the concept to Bernhard von Langenbeck's 1869 proposal and Alessandro Codivilla's 1905 attempt to lengthen malformed legs, which had high rates of infection, tissue death and nonunion. Wolfgang Rosenthal used the principle in the jaw in 1930, but it was not pursued until the 1980s.[11] Gavriil Ilizarov studied the method from the 1950s onwards in thousands of patients, developed external fixation devices and determined suitable separation rates, which led to wide adoption.[11] McCarthy and colleagues' 1992 paper on gradual mandibular lengthening began the modern craniofacial era, and reports of maxillary distraction followed in 1997 and 1998.[1][2][3][11]

Distraction osteogenesis proceeds in phases: an osteotomy and device placement, a latency period of about seven days, an activation phase in which the segments are separated by roughly 1 mm per day, and a consolidation phase while new bone matures, after which the device is removed in a second operation.[11] One description of maxillary use reports advancements of about 8-15 mm and stable bite and speech improvement in cleft patients, with vector control considered essential.[12]

Devices may be external, such as the rigid external frames described in the 1990s cleft literature,[1][2] or internal. External devices allow monitoring and adjustment but carry pin-site infection and scarring risk, according to one summary.[12]

Wikipedia describes the distraction rate as critical: too fast can lead to nonunion with fibrous tissue, too slow to premature union, and the daily 1 mm is usually split into two steps. Devices are turned manually, driven by springs or, for limb lengthening, motorised.[11] Reports in cleft patients stress that the direction (vector) of pull must be controlled.[12]

Reports describe maxillary distraction in children in mixed dentition with cleft lip and palate and in prognathic patients, aiming at aesthetic and functional benefit.[3] Another series analyzed cephalometric results in 14 cleft patients.[4] Studies have examined changes in speech[9] and in the soft-tissue profile at one year[10] after distraction. A pilot study combined adeno-tonsillectomy with rapid maxillary distraction in pre-pubertal children.[8]

A 2006 study compared cleft maxillary distraction with orthognathic surgery on morbidity and relapse,[6] and a 2010 study followed stability over five years.[7] A 2013 systematic review, cited by Wikipedia, found low-quality evidence comparing the two, with both approaches potentially effective and distraction possibly reducing long-term relapse.[13]

For appearance, a 2000 study examined soft tissue profile changes one year after maxillary advancement with distraction,[10] and a study of speech changes followed patients after distraction.[9] Wikipedia's summary of the Cochrane review reports that both approaches produced notable hard and soft tissue improvement, with no difference in speech, nasal emissions or adverse effects, and that satisfaction with distraction was lower at three months but higher at two years.[11] Evidence on distraction in the lower jaw is described as too variable to pool, with vertical relapse noted.[11]

Across craniofacial distraction generally, complications reported include infection (about 5% overall), unintended bone growth direction (7-9%), hardware failure (3-4.5%) and protocol deviations.[11] Pin-site infection in a wide range of sites and device failure are also described.[12] Relapse and the need for later orthognathic surgery are discussed in cleft studies.[6][7]
Wikipedia's figures for craniofacial distraction also include inferior alveolar nerve damage in about 3.5% of mandibular cases, tooth bud injury in about 2% and facial nerve injury in about 0.5%.[11]

Published human studies are mostly case series and comparative cohorts in cleft and hypoplasia patients.[1][2][3][4][6][7] Registered trials include a phase 2 comparison of cleft orthognathic surgery and distraction (n=60),[14] a study of rigid fixation after device removal and relapse (n=20),[15] and an observational comparison of tooth-borne, bone-borne and hybrid distraction after surgically assisted expansion (n=90).[16] No studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity were found.

Distraction osteogenesis is also used for limb lengthening, and Wikipedia describes high demand for cosmetic limb lengthening in India, where height is valued in marriage and career, alongside reports of infections, extra surgeries and patients saying they were misled about risks; China banned limb lengthening in 2006 after serious side effects.[11] Those uses involve the legs rather than the jaw, but show how the same technique has entered appearance-driven surgery. Research directions listed include shape-memory alloy devices, motor-driven distractors and combining devices with growth-factor biologics.[11]

card.summary: Gradual upper-jaw lengthening with a bone-stretching device, studied mainly in cleft and severe hypoplasia cases rather than cosmetic use.
card.note: Evidence comes from cleft and deformity patients; cosmetic use in people without a deformity has not been studied.

quick.overview:
In maxillary distraction, the upper jaw is cut and then slowly pulled forward by a device so new bone forms in the gap. It is used mainly for severe upper-jaw underdevelopment such as in cleft lip and palate.

Studies compare it with conventional advancement for relapse and stability; a Cochrane review found too little evidence for general conclusions.
quick.mechanism: After a cut, a latency of about a week, and activation at roughly 1 mm per day, a consolidation period lets the new bone mature before the device is removed.
quick.risks: Reported complications include infection, unintended direction of bone growth, hardware failure and, in craniofacial distraction generally, nerve injury. External devices carry pin-site infection and scarring risks.

chain: Upper jaw is cut and a distractor is fitted
Device separates the segments about 1 mm per day so new bone fills the gap
More forward upper jaw, fuller midface profile and corrected bite
angle.text: MDO is used for large forward movements of the upper jaw. The published use is in cleft and severe hypoplasia patients, and forum discussions treat it as a larger-scale alternative to a one-stage Le Fort I advancement.
